newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Voting ends peacefully in test-case Nigerian poll.
newsitem.headline: Voting ends peacefully in test-case Nigerian poll.

text.p: Nigerians voted peacefully on Saturday in local elections seen as a test of the military government's plan to relinquish power to civilians next year.
The elections commissioner lauded voter turnout and the government spokesmen said this showed support for military ruler General Sani Abacha's controversial democracy programme.

Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro said the vote was "an endorsement" of Abacha's civil-rule programme, dismissed by opponents as a sham. The army aborted a similar move four years ago when it scrapped a presidential poll as a winner emerged.
"The turnout of the people has been very impressive and encouraging," elections chief Sumner Dagogo-Jack told reporters.
Vote counting started at polling stations across the country after polls closed at 4 p.m. (1500 GMT). There was no immediate report of any serious incident from any of Nigeria's 36 states.
An indication of how the five registered parties performed should emerge by Sunday but full results will take a couple of days, officials said.
Dago-Jack gave no turnout figures but witnesses said polling was generally lighter in the commercial capital Lagos and outlying provinces, the bastion of opposition to the military.
"The whole transition plan is patchy," insisted leading pro-democracy campaigner Ayo Obe on Saturday. "Voters don't even know people they are voting for nor do they know the parties."
The poll to elect chairmen and councillors to more than 770 town halls is the first multi-party ballot since 1993.
The military abruptly scrapped the June 1993 presidential poll as Moshood Abiola, a business tycoon coasted to victory.
Abacha seized power in the confusion that ensued, but Nigeria plunged further into crisis after Abiola was detained in June 1994 for proclaiming himself president.
The army has ruled Nigeria for most of the time since independence from Britain in 1960. There has been widespread skepticism about the military's promise to step down in 1998.

Speculation is rife that Abacha will not hand over power to a civilian president, unless he is the civilian. Abacha insists the army will keep its promise to return to barracks, but has so far avoided addressing the burning issue of his own future.
Pro-democracy groups did not urge a boycott but nor did they show any enthusiasm for the ballot.

Voting started off on time but slowly in Lagos, with only trickles of voters noticeable at most polling stations. Officials said this was because there were many more polling stations this time than in last year's non-party elections.

Polling in the capital Abuja started on schedule but rowdy scenes erupted at some polling stations where voters complained their names were missing from voter lists or that numbers on their cards did not match those on the register.
Residents reported heavy turnout in Bauchi state in northern Nigeria, where support for the transition programme is strong. Abacha, like most of Nigeria's rulers, is from the north.
No established international or Western monitoring groups was invited to observe the elections although a 38-member U.S. team of mostly African Americans arrived this week.
The government has been shunned by Western powers since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
The National Electoral Commission of Nigeria (NECON) released final figures showing nearly 56 million voters had been registered for the poll from a population of about 100 million.
